lines.cap: **Narrator:** This is Kavya. She is twelve. Tomorrow, she has a Science test on the periodic table.
**Narrator:** It is eleven p.m. She has been staring at this poster for forty minutes.
**Kavya:** Sodium is **Na**. Potassium is **K**. Who is doing the spelling here?
**Narrator:** But this documentary is not about Kavya. It is about the poster.
**Narrator:** Look closely. It is not a table. It is a block of flats. One hundred and eighteen flats, one **element** in each.
**Silas:** Oh. The film crew. Hi. Silas. **Silicon**. I'm the caretaker.
**Sonny:** SILAS! There's a cup of WATER on the void deck! Can I touch it?!
**Silas:** No, Sonny.
**Silas:** That was sodium. You'll meet him. Sorry in advance.
**Narrator:** Block 118. Episode five: Mind the Gap.
**Silas:** Every resident here is an **element**: made of only **one kind of atom**. No chemical reaction can break it down into anything simpler.
**Narrator:** Flats are numbered by **atomic number**, or **proton number**: the number of protons in each atom.
**Harold:** Flat one. **Hydrogen**. One proton. Harold.
**Helena:** Flat two. **Helium**. Two protons. No photographs, darling.
**Kavya:** Hang on. Isn't it in order of how **heavy** they are?
**Silas:** Everyone thinks that. It's **atomic number**, not mass. Go by mass and some land in the wrong family.
**Narrator:** Every letterbox shows the element's **symbol**, **name**, **atomic number** and **mass number**.
**Silas:** Sodium's letterbox. Symbol **Na**, from his Latin name, natrium. Atomic number **11**. Mass number **23**.
**Narrator:** A column of flats is a **group**, like a stack in an HDB block. A row is a **period**, like a floor.
**Silas:** Period one is the top row. So the first floor is at the top. The building was designed by chemists.
**Narrator:** Annual flat inspection. Flat eleven: sodium.
**Sonny:** SILAS, my man! Sonny! **Sodium**! Come in, come in! Mind the oil!
**Narrator:** Every atom is like a flat. In the middle: a tiny **nucleus**, of **protons** and **neutrons**.
**Silas:** **Protons** are **positive**. **Neutrons** have **no charge**. They just sit there, adding weight.
**Narrator:** Around it, tiny **negative** **electrons** move in **shells**.
**Silas:** **Atomic number**: the number of **protons**. It decides which element you are.
**Silas:** **Mass number** is **protons plus neutrons**. Electrons are too light to count.
**Kavya:** So he has twenty-three neutrons?
**Silas:** You **subtract**. 23 − 11 = **12 neutrons**.
**Sonny:** Eleven electrons too! Same as my protons! The charges cancel!
**Narrator:** Flat six: carbon-12 and carbon-14. Both: **6 protons**. But **6 neutrons** and **8 neutrons**.
**Silas:** Same element, different numbers of neutrons: **isotopes**. Same flat, same reactions.
**Silas:** Electrons fill shells from the inside out: up to **2** in the first, **8** in the second, **8** in the third.
**Sonny:** So I'm **2, 8, 1**! And that ONE outer electron? Up for grabs!
**Sonny:** Free electron! Free electron! Anyone? Free electron!
**Silas:** He's handed it out since the day he moved in. Like the flyer guy at the MRT.
**Silas:** Same stack, same layout: everyone in a **group** has the **same number of outer electrons**.
**Sonny:** Lithium upstairs, me, Potassium downstairs! One outer electron each! FAMILY!
**Narrator:** **Outer electrons** decide how an atom reacts. So a group shares **similar chemical properties**.
**Silas:** **Group number** = number of outer electrons. Group 1: one. Group 7: seven.
**Harold:** One outer electron, like them. But I'm a gas. They never invite me.
**Silas:** Harold is the most common element in the universe. And somehow, still the loneliest.
**Narrator:** A **period** tells you the **number of shells**.
**Chloe:** Hi! Chloe! **Chlorine**! I'm **2, 8, 7**! Seven outer electrons, so **Group 7**! Three shells, so **Period 3**!
**Chloe:** I'm ONE electron away from a full outer shell. ONE! Anybody?
**Sonny:** Me! Me! I have one!
**Silas:** Not in this scene.
**Narrator:** **Metals** live on the **left** and in the **centre**. **Non-metals**, on the **right**.
**Silas:** Between them, a zig-zag line: the **staircase**. That's where I live.
**Silas:** I'm a **metalloid**. A bit of both. I get complaints from both sides.
**Narrator:** Metals are **shiny**, **good conductors**, **malleable** and **ductile**. Most are solids with **high melting points**.
**Narrator:** Non-metals are often **dull** and **brittle**, many are **gases**, and they're **poor conductors**.
**Silas:** Except **graphite**, a form of carbon: a non-metal that **conducts electricity**. There's always one.
**Narrator:** Group 1: the **alkali metals**. **Lithium**, **sodium** and **potassium**.
**Silas:** The oil? Alkali metals react with the **oxygen** and **water** in air. So they're **stored under oil**.
**Sonny:** And I'm so **soft**, you can cut me with a knife! Go on!
**Silas:** I'm not cutting you, Sonny.
**Narrator:** They're so light, they even **float** on water.
**Sonny:** Did somebody say... WATER?!
**Narrator:** **Lithium** fizzes gently.
**Narrator:** **Sodium** melts into a shiny ball and whizzes across the surface.
**Sonny:** WHEEEEEEE!
**Narrator:** **Potassium** reacts so fast, the hydrogen catches fire, with a **lilac** flame.
**Harold:** And the gas that comes off? **Hydrogen**. Me. Nobody ever says thank you.
**Silas:** **Sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen**. Sodium hydroxide makes the water **alkaline**.
**Narrator:** So reactivity **increases** as you go **down** Group 1.
**Kavya:** Why would the big ones be MORE dramatic?
**Silas:** Going down, atoms get **bigger**, so the outer electron is **further from the nucleus**.
**Silas:** And the inner shells get in the way: **shielding**. The nucleus can barely hold on.
**Sonny:** So the outer electron is **lost more easily**! Potassium throws his at people!
**Narrator:** Next door, **Group 2**, like magnesium and calcium: **two** outer electrons. Reactive, but **less** than Group 1.
**Narrator:** Group 7: the **halogens**. Reactive **non-metals**, with **seven** outer electrons.
**Chloe:** And we go everywhere in pairs! Chlorine gas is **Cl₂**. This is my other half. She's also me.
**Narrator:** **Fluorine**: **pale yellow gas**. **Chlorine**: **green-yellow gas**. **Bromine**: **red-brown liquid**. **Iodine**: **dark grey solid**, **purple** vapour.
**Silas:** Gas, gas, liquid, solid: melting points **rise** going down.
**Narrator:** Now the twist. Reactivity **decreases** down Group 7. The **opposite** of Group 1.
**Chloe:** My auntie, Fluorine, upstairs, is the most reactive. We don't visit.
**Kavya:** Wait. Group 1 gets MORE reactive going down, and Group 7 gets LESS?
**Silas:** Halogens react by **gaining** an electron. Lower down, it lands **further** from the nucleus, behind more **shielding**: a **weaker grip**.
**Silas:** Group 1 **loses** an electron: a weak grip helps. Group 7 **gains** one: a weak grip hurts.
**Narrator:** Meanwhile: Sonny and Bromine, project partners. Together, **sodium bromide**.
**Chloe:** Excuse me, Bromine. I'm **more reactive** than you. Move.
**Narrator:** A more reactive halogen **displaces** a less reactive one from its compound. The solution turns **orange**.
**Silas:** **Chlorine + sodium bromide → sodium chloride + bromine**.
**Sonny:** Chloe! You need one electron! I have ONE electron!
**Chloe:** SONNY!
**Narrator:** Sodium gives chlorine its outer electron. Both now have **full outer shells**. Together: **sodium chloride**.
**Kavya:** Wait. Sodium chloride is **salt**. That's on my chicken rice.
**Silas:** An exploding metal plus a poisonous gas equals your lunch. Chemistry is weird.

chapters.title: The penthouse and the empty flat

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Top floor, far right. The penthouse. **Group 0**: the **noble gases**.
**Helena:** We don't react, darling. My outer shell is **full**: two electrons. Neon is **2, 8**. Argon, **2, 8, 8**.
**Narrator:** A full outer shell is very **stable**: nothing to gain, lose or share. So they're **unreactive**, or **inert**.
**Sonny:** Hey, Helena! Free electron?
**Helena:** No thank you, darling. I'm **full**.
**Kavya:** So noble gases don't react because their outer shell is **empty**?
**Helena:** EMPTY?! **Full**, darling. FULL.
**Helena:** And terribly useful. Helium is lighter than air and can't burn: **balloons**. It also chills **MRI scanners**.
**Narrator:** **Neon** glows **orange-red** in signs. **Argon** fills light bulbs, and protects hot metal in **welding**.
**Silas:** That's Ah Gong. Argon. On that stool since eighteen ninety-four. Never reacted to anything.
**Narrator:** In 1869, the Russian chemist **Dmitri Mendeleev** drew up the plans for this block.
**Narrator:** He grouped elements by their properties, and where the pattern broke, he **left gaps**.
**Silas:** Empty flats, for elements not yet found. And he **predicted** what they'd be like.
**Silas:** The flat below mine sat empty for years. The listing: grey, atomic mass about 72.
**Gemma:** Hi! Gemma! **Germanium**! Grey, mass 72.6! I'm here about the flat?
**Narrator:** Germanium turned up in 1886, just as predicted: **evidence** of a **real pattern** in nature.
**Silas:** Please mind the gap.

chapters.title: The residents save you some marks

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Before the credits, the residents would like to save you some marks.
**Silas:** One. The table is in order of **atomic number**, the number of protons. **Not** mass.
**Gemma:** Two. Atomic number is the **smaller** number. For neutrons, do **mass number minus atomic number**.
**Kavya:** Three. **Groups** are **columns**, going down. **Periods** are **rows**, going across. I've GOT this.
**Sonny:** Four! Group 1 metals are **super reactive**, and reactivity **increases** down Group 1!
**Chloe:** Five! But it **decreases** down Group 7! Opposite! Don't mix us up!
**Helena:** Six. Noble gases are unreactive because their outer shell is **full**. Not empty. **Full**, darling.
**Harold:** Seven. Group 1 metal plus water gives off **hydrogen**. Me. Please, remember me.
**Narrator:** Block 118 will return.
**Silas:** So, Ah Gong. Anything you'd like to add?
**Ah Gong:** ...No reaction.
**Silas:** That's the first thing he's said since eighteen ninety-four.
